title: Net ionic equations and reaction types (AP); Limiting reagent and yield; Titrations and solution calculations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AM09#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM11#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM11#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM09#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM08#N.11, AM08b#N.3, AM09#N.4b, AM11#N.4, AM08#N.13, AM08b#N.5, AM09#N.6, AM11#N.9, AM08#N.14, AM08b#N.10, AM11#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Excess reactant
items.clue: The starting substance of which some is left over at the end.

items.label: Precipitation
items.clue: Reaction type in which dissolved ions combine into an insoluble solid.

items.label: Redox
items.clue: Reaction type in which electrons are transferred and oxidation numbers change.

items.label: Theoretical yield
items.clue: The maximum mass of product, calculated from the substance that runs out first.

questions.stem: Now the mission: vinegar. A 10.0 mL sample of vinegar is titrated with 0.500 M NaOH, using phenolphthalein. The endpoint is reached after 16.60 mL. CH₃COOH(aq) + NaOH(aq) → CH₃COONa(aq) + H₂O(l). What is the molarity of acetic acid in the vinegar?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.500 × 0.01660 = 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol. Ratio 1 : 1, so 8.30 × 10⁻³ mol of acid. Divide by the vinegar volume, 0.0100: 0.830.

questions.stem: In a back titration, an insoluble carbonate is added to excess hydrochloric acid, and the leftover acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide. Which amount equals the moles of HCl that reacted with the carbonate?

options.text: The moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid
The moles of HCl added to the solid at the very start
The moles of HCl added minus the moles of NaOH used in the titre
Half the moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid

questions.explanation: HCl reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH, so n(NaOH) = acid left over. Subtract it from the acid added to get the acid the carbonate used.

questions.stem: A 12.0 g sample of Mg(s) and 12.0 g of O₂(g) are allowed to react according to the equation 2 Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2 MgO(s). Which statement about the limiting reactant is correct and correctly justified?

options.text: Mg is limiting, because its 0.494 mol needs only 0.247 mol of O₂, and 0.375 mol of O₂ is present
O₂ is limiting, because fewer moles of O₂ (0.375 mol) than of Mg (0.494 mol) are present
O₂ is limiting, because its coefficient (1) is smaller than the coefficient of Mg (2)
Neither is limiting, because both reactants are completely converted into MgO

questions.stem: When aqueous solutions of AgNO₃ and (NH₄)₂CrO₄ are mixed, a red precipitate forms. Which of the following is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction?

options.text: 2 NO₃⁻(aq) + 2 NH₄⁺(aq) → 2 NH₄NO₃(s)
CrO₄²⁻(aq) + Ag₂⁺(aq) → Ag₂CrO₄(s)
CrO₄²⁻(aq) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Ag₂CrO₄(s)
NO₃⁻(aq) + Ag⁺(aq) → AgNO₃(s)

questions.explanation: The precipitate cannot be NH₄NO₃, so it is the other new pairing, Ag₂CrO₄. Two Ag⁺ balance the 2− charge of one CrO₄²⁻; NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectators.

questions.stem: A student titrates a 25.00 mL sample of a weak acid, HA, with 0.100 M NaOH and records the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point. The student then titrates an identical 25.00 mL sample of HA to which 50.0 mL of distilled water has been added. How does the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point in the second titration compare with that in the first, and why?

options.text: It increases, because the flask now holds a larger volume of solution
It is unchanged, because the moles of HA in the flask are unchanged
It decreases, because the HA in the flask is now more dilute
It is unchanged, because adding water does not alter the pH

questions.stem: A 10.0 mL sample of vinegar is diluted to 100.0 mL in a volumetric flask. A 25.00 mL portion needs 20.75 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O. What was the molarity of acetic acid in the original vinegar?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02075 = 2.075 × 10⁻³ mol = n(acid) in the portion. 2.075 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0830 diluted; × 10 = 0.830 in the vinegar.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the theoretical yield of a product in a reaction?

options.text: The mass of product actually obtained at the end of the experiment
The total mass of all the reactants put in, since mass is conserved
The mass of product calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant
The mass of product calculated from the reactant with the smaller number of moles

questions.explanation: The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product, from the limiting reactant and the mole ratio, assuming complete reaction and no losses.

questions.stem: Zinc metal reacts with hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2 HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). A student claims that this is an oxidation-reduction reaction. Which of the following best evaluates the claim?

options.text: The claim is correct, because the oxidation number of zinc rises from 0 to +2
The claim is correct, because each zinc atom gains 2 electrons to form Zn²⁺
The claim is incorrect, because any reaction of an acid is acid-base instead
The claim is incorrect, because there is not a species that gains or loses oxygen

questions.explanation: Zn goes 0 → +2 and H goes +1 → 0. Oxidation numbers change, so electrons are transferred (Zn to H⁺): redox.

questions.stem: Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide. Ca(OH)₂(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l). A 25.0 mL sample of limewater is titrated with 0.0500 M HCl, using phenolphthalein. The endpoint is reached after 18.40 mL. What is the molarity of the calcium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.0500 × 0.01840 = 9.20 × 10⁻⁴ mol. One Ca(OH)₂ reacts with two HCl: n = 4.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Divide by the sample volume, 0.0250: 0.0184.

questions.stem: An impure sample of magnesium oxide, an insoluble base, is analysed by back titration. MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Assume the impurities do not react with acid. A 0.400 g sample is added to 25.0 mL of 1.00 M HCl (excess). The leftover acid needs 14.30 mL of 0.500 M NaOH. What is the percentage by mass of MgO in the sample? (Molar masses: O 16.00 g/mol, Mg 24.31 g/mol)

Colourless sodium hydroxide solution is added to blue copper(II) sulfate solution. A pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, Cu(OH)₂, forms. Which is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction?

options.text: 2 Na⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Na₂SO₄(s)
CuSO₄(aq) + 2 NaOH(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq)
Cu²⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → CuOH(s)
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)

questions.explanation: Only Cu²⁺ and OH⁻ change: they pack into the solid. Atoms and charge (2+ and 2−) balance. Copper stays +2, so this is precipitation, not redox.
